implementationWaves.label: Theme runtime and native preview foundation
implementationWaves.goal: Make GPUI emitted tokens, theme switching, and review-shell navigation visible enough to support side-by-side inspection.

implementationWaves.label: Structural, action, field, selection, and overlay primitives
implementationWaves.goal: Build the GPUI primitive foundation needed to stop later composites from inventing one-off native UI semantics.

implementationWaves.label: Browse, detail, picker, table, and media composites
implementationWaves.goal: Bring the major application composites into GPUI once the primitive base is stable enough to carry them honestly.

implementationWaves.label: Command and workstation-shell parity
implementationWaves.goal: Implement the generic workstation layer that Loophole-style shared shells actually depend on.

reasons: The GPUI preview app needs section navigation and ownership context if side-by-side review is going to be credible.
This is a review shell, not a shared runtime component family.
Form semantics and validation posture are one of the strongest contract-owned surfaces.
Loophole-facing shared UI will expose form differences immediately.
Structured data parity matters, but table semantics and virtualization will likely need more native adaptation than forms or detail views.
Browse, filtering, and shell posture are important, but host and runtime-specific list behavior may require explicit deltas.
Detail surfaces are a strong contract-owned UI target and should stay close across runtimes.
This section is visually stable enough to make side-by-side parity defects obvious.
Picker and relation workflows are important, but focus scope and active-item behavior need explicit native handling.
Media shells matter for parity, but browser embed behavior and native preview capabilities are not expected to match one-to-one.
Banner, toast, skeleton, and remediation posture are shared-state surfaces that should feel materially the same across runtimes.
Command discovery is one of the clearest Loophole-facing shared workstation surfaces.
A side-by-side GPUI review surface will make ranking, grouping, and focus issues much easier to detect.
The workstation shell is the most important shared Loophole-facing UI target above primitives and composites.
This is the strongest place to prove Flint can build the same UI in Svelte and GPUI.
Token and theme parity is the floor for everything else.
This section should exist in both review surfaces before broader GPUI UI work begins.
A searchable token inspector will make parity debugging much faster even if the native presentation differs from the browser.

nonGoals: Do not treat DOM-specific implementation details as mandatory when the contract can be satisfied more honestly by a GPUI-native approach.
Do not reopen Loophole-specific DAW widget ownership under the banner of GPUI parity.
Do not claim GPUI parity from token emission or preview-app scaffolding alone.
